House in Committee on Bill (No. 161) respecting the incorporation of Joint Stock Companies by letters patent.-The Prime Minister.

Mr. Chairman, the Bill which is before the committee, the Joint Stock Companies Bill, is a formidable-looking one, but in reality the changes that are proposed in the law are comparatively few. I may say that the object of the government in introducing this Bill was to bring the position respecting incorporation of joint stock companies into a state somewhat more in accordance with
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR. (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

speechtext:
the requirements of modern business. It is our opinion that the law, as it at present stands upon the statute-book and the practice in regard to the incorporation of joint stock companies, is altogether cumbrous, unsatisfactory and out of date, and any member of the legal profession who has had anything to do with the incorporation of companies under the Joint Stock Companies Act of the Dominion, will agree that it requires amendment. The principle that is being followed now in countries where business is carried on under modern conditions is, that, hi respect to that class of companies which ,ean be described as industrial companies every possible facility should be given for incorporation, that incorporation should be made as speedy, as free from unnecessary difficulty and as inexpensive as possible. This is the most important object which we have in view in connection with the Bill which is now before us. The general provisions constituting the law respecting joint stock companies are not substantially changed, and the number of new sections is very few.
The effect of the law as it exists at the present time has been to drive the business away from the federal government. Persons have been compelled to go to the various provinces and the various states of the Union for the purpose of getting charters of incorporation. It will be agreed by the House that we should have our law in such a state that persons would not have to go somewhere else to get a charter to do business in Canada. The Bill was introduced in the Senate because it was thought that the Senate would perhaps give more time to the consideration of its various clauses than would perhaps be possible in this House. If any hon. gentleman thinks mat a substantial change is required in any particular section, he might perhaps give the matter due deliberation, and bring an amendment if necessary next session. Our desire is that the Bill should be gone through with now, so that the proceedings for incorporating joint stock companies may be put upon a more modern and up-to-date basis. This subject of joint stock incorporation has received a great deal of attention, both in England and in the United States, and I think that the English system is perhaps the most simple of any. The principle of this Act is to some extent followed in this Bill. Most of the sections will be found just as they were in the old law. The second section is new, but it simply declares what companies the Act should apply to. The 5th section says : ' That upon an application being made by persons, not less than live in number, the Secretary of State may issue a charter.' It obviates a long process of advertising, and the passing from one department to the other, and is somewhat similar to the English law. Section 13 is
new, and it enables persons who have been incorporated in any province or in a foreign country to get incorporated under Dominion charter, so that if people have been incorporated in the province of Ontario and desire to do business in another province, they can come here, and without expensive legislation get a charter from the Dominion, In the same way, if they become incorporated in the United States, with the object of doing business in Canada, they can get a Canadian charter. Proper precautions have been taken in the section to prevent any abuses. Section 18 provides that the company shall not commence its operations until ten per cent of its authorized capital has been subscribed and paid for. The provisions of the Joint Stock Companies Act in the past have been for the purpose of preventing companies starting in business until they had taken steps to put themselves in a bona tide position to do so. Many of the provisions in the existing law are in effect ludicrous. For instance, the provision which requires that a company had to pay a certain amount of money before they got their incorporation has at least the merit of age. But every lawyer knows that it is a common practice to borrow money from the banks to make the deposit, and when the incorporation is issued they get the cheque back. This section requires that ten per cent shall be bona tide subscribed before the business is begun, and it seems to provide all the safeguards that can be provided in a case of this kind. Section 35 provides that the corporation shall not make use of its funds for the purchase of stock in other corporations, unless and until a by-law for that purpose has been passed by two-thirds of the value of the stock, except the charter specifically provides otherwise that it may be done. It is claimed that the law heretofore has not been sufficiently flexible. Sometimes a trading company desires to take stock in other trading companies for the purpose of protecting themselves respecting the indebtedness of one company to the other, without incurring any liability for the general conduct of the business. Under this section, while there is a proper safeguard, they would not be prevented from taking that course. Section 46 is new. Section 57 provides for the borrowing of money by the corporation, and it is taken from the Ontario law, which received very careful consideration at the hands of corporation lawyers and of bankers, and has been found to work very satisfactorily. Section 79 provides for the inspection of the business of the company, and is new. There are two methods, one of which is that by which the shareholders representing one-quarter in value of the capital stock of the company may apply to a judge for the purpose of having an inspection of the affairs of the company made. That is for the pur-
pose of protecting the minority shareholders who might not feel that the majority were handling the business as it ought to be.
Can that inspection be required at any time ?
At any time upon the application of shareholders representing not less than one-fourth of the value of the stock.
It might be used to embarrass the company.

The application must be supported by such evidence as a judge may require for the purpose of deciding that the inspection is necessary, and it is in the discretion of a judge of the Superior Court, to whom we must leave a great deal of discretion in such a matter. Section 89 provides that returns shall be made to the government. That, I think, covers everything that is new in the Bill.
On section 13,

I objected at first to having this Bill taken up on account of the very late date in the session. The Alinister of Justice afterwards pointed out to me that a very small portion of the Bill was new, and indicated to me the sections that were new. I have not had an opportunity of verifying what portion is new and what portion is old. I take for granted that what he said in the House with regard to that is correct, and the government, of course, are responsible for the Bill. With regard to this section, I do not know whether it is taken from any existing legislation or not; but it struck me, looking at the wording of it, that there may be some difficulty in working it out. The latter part of the first subsection provides :
After the issue of the letters patent the company shall be governed in all respects by the provisions of thi3 Act, except that the liability of the shareholders to creditors of the old company shall remain as at the time of the issue of the letters patent.
A difficulty is, I believe, not unknown in the United States, in the case of companies having double charters, the provisions of which are sometimes inconsistent with each other. Certain provisions of this Act, according to this section, are to be applicable to the company, and it may be incorporated under the laws of a foreign country, which are not in all respects the same as the provisions of this Act. There may be some difficulty in working it out, but I suppose there is no harm in allowing it to pass, with the suggestion that it may be amended afterwards if that is found necessary.
The MINISTER OF THE INTERioR. That point has been pretty well considered in the course of dealing with the incorporation of joint stock companies. The provinces have laws authorizing the granting Hon. Mr. SIFTON.
of licenses to foreign corporations, and the practice under this Act would be to all intents and purposes the same as that which the provinces follow. If any difficulty occurs in the working of the Act, which is the only way in which we can find out, we can amend it from time to time.

I observe that the fees for letters patent fixed by the. Governor in Council in the past have been considerably higher than they are in some other countries. For instance, in the province of Nova Scotia, it is not unusual for people siderably higher than they are in some other well known in the shipping trade, to form a joint stock company for every one of those ships.
Do they incorporate in the province ?

They usually come here, because they send their ships ail over the world. The result is that the fees amount to a considerable sum. I brought this matter to the attention of the Secretary of State some years ago, because I thought the fees secured by the government would be more if they were somewhat lower.

There is a great deal in what my hon. friend says, and an attempt ought to be made to prepare a scheme of fees which would be commensurate with the size and Importance of the business with respect to which the incorporation is taking place, so that we could incorporate companies such as those to which my hon. friend refers at a very moderate expense.

It may be true, as the hon. Minister of the Interior has stated, that the former provisions of the law were very often evaded, or that attempts were made to evade them iD the way he mentions. I am not quite sure that these attempts would prove successful if they were really tested in a court of law.
I do not see any provision in this statute which would prevent a similar evasion in future, so that I do not know that it effects any improvement in that respect. I am not able to suggest at present any alteration in the section which would make it more secure.

The hon. gentleman will see that the Act does not profess to provide that any particular sum of money shall be paid in for the incorporation.
On section 38,

This section, by postponing the rights of the holders of common shares against their will to the rights of the holders of preference shares, might possibly work an injustice. However, I suppose you cannot provide against everything of that kind, and I have no objection to the section passing in its present form, subject

to the future possible necessity of amending it.

I think it is practically the same as the law at present.- It was amended in 1900.
On section 51,

I would like to draw the attention of the minister to the language of this section, which says that it shall not apply to companies whose stock is listed and dealt with on the stock exchange. That is rather a general expression. What does it mean exactly ? There are half a dozen stock exchanges in Canada. What would be the effect of that ?
It is very likely taken from the English Act.
The language may be taken from the English Act as there is only one stock exchange in England.
1	do not think it is taken from the English Act.	.

My hon. friend will see that subsection
2	simply removes, as regards stocks listed in the stock exchange, the prohibition provided in section 51, under which every transfer of stock must be entered in the transfer book of the company before it can be valid.
Mr. BORDEN" (Halifax). What do you mean by the term ' the stock exchange.' Suppose you have a company incorporated in Nova Scotia, where there is no stock exchange. The stock is listed in Montreal, and listed nowhere else. Is the Montreal Stock Exchange to be considered ' the stock exchange ' within the meaning of the statute or not ? Or could a transfer by means of endorsing the scrip be made inNova Scotia ?

I do not think there will be any difficulty. The by-laws of the company will provide where scrip and certificates of stock will be transferable by delivery. There is no reason why a company should not provide by a by-law that its stock scrips shall be transferable by delivery.
I think it would better carry out the idea of this section and make it a little more definite, if we were to say ' any recognized stock exchange ' instead of ' the stock exchange.'
What do you mean by a recognized stock exchange ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: The stock exchange of Montreal or Toronto.

The courts will decide that such and such a place was a recognized stock exchange, 159J
just as the courts in England decide what is an open market.

Would it not be better to use the word ' incorporated ' instead of ' recognized.' There are a number of stock exchanges which are not incorporated, and are of very inferior order to those which are incorporated. While I do not know sufficiently about the scope of the Act to say whether it is right to exclude those, I can see some inconvenience in the use of a term which might be held to apply to stock exchanges not incorporated.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: A broker will sometimes establish in his office what he calls a stock exchange, in cities where there is no recognized stock exchange, and I think the intention is to avoid legalizing transfers of scrip in such places. Probably we had better use the word ' incorporated,' as suggested by the hon. gentleman.

I do not think there would be any difficulty in practice if we were to use the term ' recognized stock exchange.' The courts are competent to decide, in cases of dispute, whether a certain stock exchange was in reality a recognized stock exchange or not. I move that this section be amended by inserting the words ' recognized stock exchange,' in place of the words, ' the stock exchange.'
Why not use the word ' incorporated ' ?

There are all sorts of Stock exchanges, and if you use the word ' recognized,' that may lead to difficulty. If you use the word ' incorporated,' there are stock exchanges where a good deal of business is carried on, which are not incorporated. If the stock is listed on a regular stock exchange, it can be dealt in by curb brokers, and a purchaser who buys innocently from a curb broker should not suffer. I do not think there is any necessity for the amendment. After a year's trial of this Act, if any amendments be thought necessary, we can make them next session. I do not think any harm will result in leaving the section as it is, and we might do some injustice by amending it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: It is rather too indefinite to talk about ' the stock exchange,' and more difficulty will likely arise if the clause be left as it is than to make some change as suggested.
If it were left open as it is, merely 'the stock exchange,' I think it would be interpreted by the court as it would appear to me to be-the incorporated stock exchanges of the various centres.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I do not think my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) quite

appreciates the conditions which may arise. For instance, in Nova Scotia we have no stock exchange as that word is ordinarily accepted. The securities of many Nova Scotia companies are listed on the Toronto or Montreal stock exchanges, and they are purchased on these exchanges by the people in Halifax. Suppose you have a case before the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia, in which this question was involved, would these words mean the Toronto Stock Exchange, or the Montreal Stock Exchange- or would they mean anything ? It would leave us in a position of very grave uncertainty. I do not think it makes much difference whether you say ' recognized ' or whether you say ' incorporated ' stock exchange, assuming that all the stock exchanges are incorporated.

I quite agree with the hon. leader of the opposition that that word ought to be defined. Particularly in view of the wild speculations in the stock markets recently, this change is a very desirable one. 1 would prefer to see the word * incorporated,' because ' recognized ' is a relative expression and vague. What would constitute ' recognition ? '
Recognition in the markets of the world.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: But what is the stamp of 1 recognition ? ' How are you to determine whether a stock exchange is ' recognized ' or not ? The word * incorporated ' is the one to use, as the stock exchanges in Montreal and Toronto are incorporated, as any other recognized stock exchange ought to be incorporated.
Is there a stock exchange in Halifax ?
Not an incorporated stock exchange.
Is there an institution carried on as a stock exchange, 'but not incorporated ?

The brokers, who have a very extensive business, call themselves the ' Halifax Stock Exchange,' or something of that kind. There is no place where brokers meet and go through the usual manoeuvres that brokers do on first-class stock exchanges, as in some of the larger cities of the continent ; but they carry on operations by purchasing in New York, Montreal, or Toronto.
Practically, they are brokers ?
Yes.
The difficulty about using the word ' incorporated ' is simply that a company might be incorporated under the name of a stock exchange, yet have no substantial standing in the country whatever.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Then, say ' recognized and incorporated.'
I have not followed this discussion, but, if this refers to mining exchanges, I would point out that we have a very important mining exchange in Montreal, and I do not think it is incorporated.
Is it not part of the Canadian Mining Institute, which is an incorporated body ?
No.
They surely must be incorporated, otherwise they could not carry on business.
They carry on business in Montreal, but they are not incorporated. The stock exchange is incorporated, but not this mining exchange.

I should think the word ' recognized ' might bear the burden for a year. My hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) suggests that it has no very definite meaning, but the position of the Prime Minister of this country is constituted by a word in the statute-book very much the same.
OF THE INTERIOR Words that no difficulty is found in interpreting.
I agree with the hon. Minister of the Interior, but we might use the word ' recognized ' and thus get over difficulties such as the one suggested by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk).

speechtext: ['I have no fault to find with the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd). He will of course understand that it was only at the expiration of the year 1901 that this question came up for consideration.\nResolutions reported, read the first and second time and agreed to.']

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RAILWAY EXTENSION IN NOYA SCOTIA.
speechtext: As the work on the Halifax and South-western Railway is about to be commenced, I desire to offer a few remarks in that connection, interested as I naturally am in the road which is to pass through the county I have the honour to represent.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RAILWAY EXTENSION IN NOYA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend allow me to make a suggestion '!

X was proposing that the House go into Committee of Ways and Means for the purpose of disposing of the Supply Bill, for which the Senate is waiting, and if my bon. friend desires to make any observations, we will afford him an opportunity after that is over.
Mr. IvAULBACII. I will only be a few minutes. The Nova Scotia Southern Railway, better known as the Hervey lane, was started, if I remember rightly, in 1894, upon which it is reported $400,000 was expended in preliminary surveys and construction, but owing to an interference or friction between the promoter of it and the Coast Railway Company-a war of route, if it may be so called-and the Dominion and Nova Scotia governments, not having sufficient decision to give the Hervey line so called the preference, it being the'first that was subsidized, operations were suspended pending results. I am very desirous, nevertheless, that a road shall be built between Halifax and Shelburne, and properly located where it will open a country for settlement, and develop the resources for the farmers, miners and lumbermen. Some would say, locate the road where it will give convenience to the greatest number, meaning along the shore. This would serve the purpose for Halifax and Shelburne counties very well, as these counties, unfortunately, have little or no farming country in both, the settlers being on the shore, but I am happy to say it is not the case with Lunenburg and Queen's, as the interior of these counties possesses the very finest of land for farming, suitable for producing anything that can be raised in Canada, and for purposes of fruit growing cannot be excelled, settled by a thrifty people, the places being known as Caledonia, South Brookfield, North Brookfield, Pleasant River, Hempford, Ohio, New Germany, Poster Settlement and New Ross, which are villages and settlements thrifty and full of promise, awaiting the completion of the Hervey road. How are these places to be reached, I would ask, if the proposed road is to follow the shore route, where the settlers have now all the facilities for travel by water and for the transport of ail their sea and soil products ? I say that the settlers referred to, attracted to the rich agricultural lands in the interior of Lunenburg and Queen's, who have made homes for themselves and their families, are they to be refused a road to a market, places proverbially well suited for agriculture and horticulture, with lakes and streams to beautify the scene, well supplied with fish to attract the sportsman, and as I said, for richness of soil and adaptability for agriculture and fruit growing is not surpassed by the far-famed reputation of Annapolis and King's county valleys, nor in any part of Canada ?
The interior also possesses rich productive gold mines, notably the Libby, Maliga and
numerous others, as well as other mineral deposits, as also valuable timber of hard and soft wood, stretching from the confines of Halifax and Lunenburg counties in the east to Shelburne in the west, all awaiting railway facilities to reach a market. This country, rich as I have described in natural resources and other advantages, should be considered in the location of this road, more particularly as the right of way can be had ' without money and without price,' as we all have agreed to give the lands required for the road without charge, whereas by the shore road a tax will be exacted. As to the cost of construction of the road through the interior, as compared with the shore route, I feel safe in saying, as I have been advised, that there is a difference of 40 per cent in favour of the interior, as the interior has only brooks instead of rivers to cross, and the country moderately undulating, or almost a level, with few cuttings, and that alluvial, and a straight route with little expense for bridging, as the bridges would be little better than culverts, as the streams are light. Whilst the shore route would require heavy bridging, precipitous cross hills to overcome, which means moving around them, thereby necessitating a more expensive, circuitous, and necessarily a longer route.
Now, Mr. Speaker, after this brief review of the situation, as to the location of the proposed interior route, as compared with the shore route, you will permit me to state that I am familiar with the geography of the counties through which this proposed road will pass, and the locations of the two proposed routes, so far as projected surveys have been made, and the rich and varied resources and advantages of the interior route as compared with the other, and possessing this knowledge, I feel it my duty to give it to the country and the public free of any personal or political bias. My view as to route is as follows : Start from the city of Halifax at a convenient point for passenger and freight traffic, and from thence on a line as straight as possible for the head waters of St. Margaret's Bay and Hubert's Cove, and thence for Chester, Chester Basin, and Gold River, thence following the valley of said Gold River, which is all but a straight line, as far as New Ross, thence straight for Shelburne via Foster Settlement, New Germany,'Ohio, Hempford, Pleasant River, North 'Brookfield, South Brookfield, Caledonia and Indian Gardens- Shelburne having a harbour second' to none in the world for depth of water, easy of approach by night or day, on the shore of the blue waters of the Atlantic, with no tortuous waters, such as we encounter on the Bay of Fundy, and a harbour of refuge not to be excelled. This road would form the main artery, or trunk line from Halifax to Shelburne, and an international road as well, as by a line of steamers from Shelburne to Boston, or New York, it would be

the shorter route by five hours, anti the most delightful of any of the routes at present travelled.
By this route Hubert's Cove and Chester, the favourite resort for tourists, Chester Basin, New Ross, and the other places 1 have named, will have direct communication with either Halifax or Shelburne, they being on the main artery or belt lines, and from this belt line, branches will run to Liverpool and Lockeport, Bridgewater, Ma-hone Bav and Lunenburg, being provided for already, thus practically making each town on the shore the terminus of a railway line, and receiving the products and traffic of each branch, as also a part of the main trunk. By this method the interior of the country with its resources, will be developed, and through it encourage a population five times that we possess at present.
As the road between New Germany and Caledonia is well on towards completion, with a heavy cut stone bridge across the La Have River, now built, the heaviest on the route, with other bridges and culverts either placed in position or the cut stone and material on the grounds to build them, sleepers piled up along the beach sufficient to lav the entire road between Caledonia and New Germany, road-bed all but completed for the laying of the rails, I would therefore ask that this portion of the road be cared for at once, so that the sleepers, tending to decay, may be utilized, as a very small outlay would be called for to complete this entire section.
There is one special feature I desire to present most forcibly to the attention of the government, and that is that the local government be advised as well as themselves of the necessity and justice for the payment of back bills due to workmen and traders for labour performed, and material furnished, including sleepers, in the construction of the road between New Germany and Caledonia; that every dollar of these bills be paid, before an appropriation is made for any other purpose, as the value of the road at present is the labour that has been put into it by the workmen, and those who supplied them, and as a consequence should first be paid.
As this portion of road is so near completion, I would ask when are the contractors intending to commence work, and will the work be submitted to tender ?
I would also ask if it is the intention of the government to have the entire road between Halifax and Shelburne definitely located by survey, before any portion of construction begins ?

speechtext:
The subject of railway extension from the city of Halifax along the south shore of Nova Scotia, or through tne south-western counties of Nova Scotia, has long occupied the attention of the government, and I am 'glad to say that during the last year or two the matter has taken a Mr. KAULBACH.
much more satisfactory shape than in former years. By the co-operation of the local and Dominion governments-I put the local government first, because they are bearing the heavier end of the burden-an arrangement has been made which I feel assured will give the people of that section of the country, at a very early date, the railway construction which they have so long desired.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RAILWAY EXTENSION IN NOYA SCOTIA.
speechtext: Hear, hear. I quite endorse that.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RAILWAY EXTENSION IN NOYA SCOTIA.
speechtext:
As to the question of the rival routes-that is to say, the interior route and the shore route-I am afraid that I shall not be able to agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Kaulbach) as fully as he could desire. We gave a contract for a large portion of the railway by the interior route to a company, which failed to construct it, and we now find that the workmen who are employed on that construction are clamouring to be paid. The people interested in that interior route have had their opportunity, and unfortunately the enterprise has failed. The probability is now that the new company which takes hold of the enterprise will not build the interior route as it was originally contemplated, but will build the shore route from Halifax to Shelburne, and on to Barrington Passage, from which a road is now constructed to Yarmouth. However, a portion of the interior route has been constructed, the line starting from the village of New Germany, and running as far as the village of Caledonia Corner, in the county of Queen's. It is a fact that that portion of the road is far advanced ; it is in a condition that the expenditure of a very moderate amount of money would bring it up to the point where it could be operated. But, the bills remain unpaid. It is our strongest desire in dealing with a new company that we should bring about some arrangement whereby these bills can be paid, but we cannot expect any new contractor to pay any bills unless he gets value for them. If the value is there it will be our endeavour to use that value to pay the people who performed the work, and we will do our utmost in that direction. But. I think I must qualify that statement by saying that if there is no value to be got out of that portion of the road, I do not see how we can expect a new contractor to pay for anything he is not getting, but where he will get value, it is only right that he shall pay the money to the people whose time and energy and skill went into the work, and we shall do our utmost to see that these bills shall be paid. I anticipate that that portion of the road, although it will not form part of the main line from Halifax to Yarmoutl), will be completed at a very early date. I do not like to speak too confidently in a railway matter, because difficulties frequently occur, but I am in hope that before the present calendar year ends the twenty odd miles

between New Germany and Caledonia Corner will be completed, and will be in operation, and I am in hope that it will ultimately bs extended down as far as Liverpool. That is a matter for future consideration, and I can say nothing further about it. As to the general location, I have already stated that I believe the shore route will be preferred for several reasons. The first reason I have already given, and it is that the company which undertook to carry out the work in the interior route did not carry out the work. We have a company offering to build the shore route, and we have no company offering to build the interior route. Besides that, the local government, who have borne the heavy end of the burden, have undertaken to make an arrangement for the construction of that road, which they have made with no other company in Nova Scotia. They propose that they shall aid the company by loaning them in cash $13,200 a mile for the whole road. That aid is granted on the understanding that the line shall follow what is generally called the shore route. Of course that will have to be so located as to meet the various districts along the shore as far as possible. While we are entitled, under the terms of our contract, to reserve the right to approve of the location, still, the government realize that the local government are bearing the heavy end of the burden, and that their views ought to have very great consideration-and they will have. So much for the general question. Now, my hon. friend (Mr. Kaulbach) asks whether we shall approve of any part of the location before any work is commenced, or whether we shall require the whole of the location to be decided before the work proceeds. There are portions of the road as to which there is no question about the location, and if the company shall begin work immediately upon those portions we shall be very well satisfied, but I do not anticipate very much delay in the road being located. There is only a small portion of the road in regard to which there will be very much difficulty about the location. The general subsidy Act contains a provision which requires that these locations shall be subject to the approval of the Governor General in Council, and that approval must be applied for. As the local government are bearing the heavy burden in the matter, we are disposed to defer very largely to their views in regard to the location, not giving the matter up entirely, but still meeting them in every way possible, in order that this long delayed work may be carried out. As to the way in which the work is to be done, wlie-ther by tender or not, my hon. friend must see that as the work is to be done by a company and not by the government" we have no right to dictate to them in that respect at all. They will make the best arrangement they can, and if they can make a better arrangement by tender than
in any other way you may rely upon it that they will make it by tender ; but this is a matter for the company to do what they think proper, and one in regard to which we cannot lay down any terms.

Mr. Speaker, at an earlier stage of the session I addressed a question to the government relating to the Department of Inland Revenue ; and as I see the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue present, I would like to ask what decision has been reached by his department as to the means to be taken to prevent a recurrence of the distribution of coal oil of low illuminating power throughout Manitoba and the North-west, such as occurred during the past winter.

When my main estimates were before the House, that question of coal oil was brought up, and I promised then that I would investigate the matter and report to the House later on. In order to make the matter more clear, I will read to the House a report or memorandum [DOT]which was prepared on that subject, giving the wihole story :
(Memo.)
Ottawa, April 28, 1902.
At the end of December, 1901, the attentioa of the department was called, through the Hon. the Minister of the Interior, to complaints made in the North-west as to the inferior quality! of coal oil.
On December 30, the Hon. Mr. Sifton was informed that if a sample of the oil complained of was forwarded to the department, a chemical analysis thereof would be made.
On the 10th January, 1902, two samples -were received and submitted to the Chief Analyst for examination.	.
On the 7th January the Chief Analyst reported that from Mr. McGill's investigation it did not appear that the samples were of inferior quality. Both samples stood the tests provided by the Petroleum Inspection Act. The incrustation on the wick as well as the deposit on chimney, by burning in an ordinary lamp, was normal.
On January 18, Collector Alexander, of London, was Instructed to visit the refinery at Sarnia and personally select several samples from the stock of refined petroleum on hand, said samples to represent the highest, lowest and medium grades.
These samples were collected by Mr. Alexander from barrels ready for shipment, and represented all the grades, except high test oils.

put upon the Canadian market by the Imperial Oil Company.
On January 24, Inspector Barrett was advised of the reports that had reached the department relative to alleged bad quality of coal oil, and was requested to instruct the officers throughout his district to make a systematic inspection of oil in the hands of dealers.
Twenty-two (22) samples were collected in Winnipeg and St. Boniface, four (4) at Portage la Prairie, six (6) at Brandon, four (4) at Moosomin, one (1) at Prince Albert, three (3) at Regina, two (2) at Moosejaw, one (1) at Souris, two (2) at Deloraine, three (3) at Boissevain, two (2) at Killarney, two (2) at Manitou, three (3) at Morden, two (2) at Morris, three (3) at Fincher Creek, three (3) at Maeleod, two (2) at Lethbridge, five (5) at Calgary, four (4) at Edmonton, one (1) at Stratlnona.
In all seventy-five (75) samples were collected and tested, and in every instance the sample was found to stand the flash-test and to be; within the gravity established by the Act.
The collector at Winnipeg reported nine (9) samples as complained of by dealers. These samples were submitted to District Analyst E. B. Kenrick for chemical examination. The result of Mr. Kenrick's investigations failed to establish that any of the samples were of objectionable quality. In addition to the chemical analysis, oil from each of the nine (9) objectionable samples was burned in an ordinary lamp for six (6) hours and not noticeable incrustation was found upon the wick nor fouling upon the chimney. Mr. Collector Gosnel, cf Winnipeg, reports that he personally burned oil from these nine (9) samples and found them all to burn well except a sample obtained from Mr. Geo. Wheeler, of Winnipeg, which for seven (7) or eight (S) hours gave a good light, then became dull and practically went out. After removal of the incrustation upon the wick the lamp was again lighted and burned satisfactorily. This sample, as reported on by Mr. Kenrick, was found to contain a much larger proportion of fixed residue than any of the other samples examined, the percentage being *33, as compared with an average of '061 in the remaining eight (8) samples. The oil represented by those nine (9) samples was believed to be all of American manufacture.
The three (3) samples of Canadian oil collected at the refinery at Sarnia and examined by Mr. McGill at the laboratory in Ottawa show that they are good oils, although the more delicate instrument used by Mr. McGill showed the gravity of the '805 oil to be -8063. Mr. McGill reports that neither the deposits on the lamp chimney nor the incrustation of the wick were sufficient to sustain serious complaint against them.
A fact apparent by the examinations made by both Messrs. McGill and Kenrick was that the oils of heavy gravity contained the largest percentage of sulphur. In the Canadian samples this ranged from -03803 in the oil of '797 gravity to -07655 in that of the gravity of -805. In the sample examined by Mr. Kenrick it ranged from -0221 in an oil of a gravity of -7921 to '0365 in an oil of a gravity of -8039. In none of these cases is the percentage of sulphur as large as that permitted by law to be found in ordinary coal gas, viz., 35 grains per 100 cubic feet or, computed as in the coal, oil -147,
Any attempt made to reduce the range of gravities as now established by the Act, viz., '775 to *805 would add to the cost of production

speechtext:
and give the oil refiners a reasonable excuse for increasing the cost to the consumer.
So far as it^ was possible to ascertain, the trouble arose in connection with a lot of oil placed in storage tank No. 2 at Fort William, in July, 1901. This oil was discharged from tank barge No. 36, shipped by the Standard Oil Company, Chicago, and consigned to the Imperial Oil Company, Fort William.
This storage tank holds 10,000 barrels of oil. Mr. Inspector Barrett reports that 9,000 barrels drawn out of this tank gave perfect satisfaction but the remaining oil, taken from the bottom of the tank, did not give satisfactory results.
Mr. Barret; further reports that as soon as the Imperial Oil Company learned that complaints were made they examined the oil and found that it was unsatisfactory, inasmuch as the wick clogged after burning for a time and caused a diminution of the flame. They at once recalled the oil and paid freight both ways.
At the request of Mr. F. Oliver, M.P., further inquiries were made at Lethbridge where it was alleged serious complaints had been made. Mr. Acting-Collector Saucier advises the department under date, April 24, 1902, that he called upon the following dealers, viz. : A. McDonald & Co., II. Bentley, Hudson Bay Company, Brodie & Stafford, Sherlock & Freeman and Win. Scott.
Of the above, A. McDonald & Co. state bad oil was first noticed in October ; H. Bentley had no complaints ; Hudson Bay Company had a few complaints ; Brodie & Stafford had no complaints ; Sherlock & Freeman had received complaints in October or November and some bad oil was returned to them in December, and Wm. Scott had complaints continuously from September, 1901, to February, 1902.
The Acting Collector states that there was probably not more than one consignment of inferior oil last October and that it was on the market from the middle of October to some time in December.
In conclusion, the department is of the opinion from the reports received that a quantity of inferior oil was put upon the market late in the autumn, that as soon as the Imperial Oil Company were advised of the fact that the oil was not giving satisfaction it was recalled at the company's expense, that in all probability this inferior quality of oil was not on sale for a longer period than three months, that with the exception of this one consignment the oil supplied has given satisfaction, and that for some months past no complaints have arisen.
Attached hereto are copies if the results obtained by Messrs. McGill and Kenrick.
It will be seen, therefore, from the reports and the correspondence attached, that as soon as complaints reached the department, we did our best to collect the oil in the North-west Territories and Manitoba, and subject it to an analysis, the reports of which are contained in this return.
I do not wish the hon. minister to assume
There is no motion before the Chair.
I think there will be no objection taken to the hon. member (Mr. Oliver) speaking.
The hou. member might put himself in order by making a motion.

I move the adjournment of the House. I do not wish the hon. minister to assume, as he apparently does assume, that there was any desire to attack his department or the administration df it. But a certain condition of affairs existed, and it was felt to be in the best interest of the country as of the government that the facts should be made known, with a view to finding a remedy for that condition at the earliest possible moment. I am willing to accept the statement of the hon. minister that every effort was made by the department to arrive at a knowledge of the facts, but I am compelled to call attention to this, that the efforts made by the department through its officers were not as successful as they should have been. The hon. minister has read us a statement of the reports of his officer that would indicate that there was no bad oil sold in Manitoba or the Northwest Territories last winter. But after reading the result of these official reports, the hon. minister makes a statement from another and a higher officer who admits that at least a thousand barrels, or was it gallons ?
Barrels.
A thousand barrels of inferior oil were put upon the market.
There was ten thousand barrels of oil in the one tank. Of this, nine thousand barrels gave satisfaction, but the residue of one thousand barrels did not.

Then one thousand barrels of inferior oil were put upon the market of Manitoba and the North-west Territories last fall, and consumers were supplied with inferior oil during a period of three months. And yet the officers who were sent out into Manitoba and the North-west Territories to examine the samples of oil were not able to -did not, as a matter of fact-locate that bad oil. I am not blaming either the minister for his intentions, nor his officers, but 1 point out this, as I did in my remarks when the question was under discussion before, that the present tests for flash and gravity do not determine the illuminating power of the oil. That, I claim, is unquestionably established by the report we have had placed before us to-day. And I again call upon the hon. minister to provide in some way for some test of the oil as to its illuminating qualities. It is not as to its flash or as to its gravity that we want to know in regard to this oil ; what we want to know is whether it will give light. And, if it is a fact, as it appears to be. that the present tests do not enable the officers to judge of the illuminating quality of the oil, then we must urge upon the minister, for our own protection and for his credit, to secure such expert
ability as may be possible to provide a test that will determine whether the oil will give light or not. The facts are as he stated, that, for three months during the darkest part of last winter, the oil supplied throughout Manitoba and the North-west was of inferior illuminating powers. Whether it would stand the flash test or the gravity test is of no interest to the public. The fact is it would not stand the practical test of illumination, and we want such a test applied as will ensure that when we pay for oil we shall get light. Now, the assertion is made that the company withdrew the bad oil and paid the freight both ways. I am not in the oil business, but I am perfectly satisfied that that statement is not universally correct. What may have been done in some parts of the country I do not know, but I am perfectly satisfied that, so far as the town in which I live >s concerned, the company certainly did not withdraw the oil or pay the freight both ways.

Let me merely call attention to the fact, Mr. Speaker, that here, within twenty minutes of the close of the session, this question, the most important to the people of Manitoba and the North-west, except the transportation question, is brought up. The people of that country were to a very large extent in the dark last winter ; but here at this last moment of the session we have some light thrown on this subject. It will be most gratifying to the people of Manitoba and the North-west Territories to find at last they have this light. And the intimation is given us that we do not know anything about it. When we buy bad oil and that oil will not give light, it will be most consoling to know that we do not understand the ' gravity ' and the ' flash ' and all that business that the scientists of the department are so familiar with. The local conditions are such that we do not understand these things. But next winter, or some future time when the lamps will not burn, when the oil only blackens the glass, and sticks in the wick, we shall be able to send for some of these officers so that they may enlighten us with the explanation of the* ' gravity ' and * flash.' Or it will afford us delight to send for the Minister of Inland Revenue himself to come up. But I wish to warn him that if he comes up with the great document he has read us today and undertakes to read it, he will not be able to do so.
Why not ?

Because there will not be light enough-unless he should do as he has done to-dav, bring his report in in the middle of the day, when he will not need lamp light. The hon. minister tells us that his officers did not find any of this bad oil. And how could thev, when, according to the hon. minister the bad oil had all been brought

back ? This oil was taken into tlie country in October, and it was not until January that any practical move was made by the Department of Inland Revenue. Tlie result of it was, to use the hon. minister's own words, ' they recalled the oil and paid the freight both ways.' Then, after the oil had been recalled, the officers of the department were sent out, and, strangely enough, they were not able to find any of the bad oil in tlie country.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me a second ?	-
Certainly, a whole minute.

I merely desire to repeat that the first I11-timation that the department had was received from the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) in December, and it was acted upon at once. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyd) knew the facts. If he had given us information of the facts earlier, we certainly would have taken action earlier.

Why, the facts were published broadcast in the press and discussed everywhere. And, in the first place, it was the fault of the officers of the Minister of Customs that the oil was allowed to come into the country. If it was necessary, in order to rectify their error, to notify the Department of Inland Revenue, why did they not do so ? But no, the information must come from a member of parliament and be communicated to the Minister of the Interior, and so be passed on up to the Department of Inland Revenue. I say it does not lie in the mouth of the Minister of Inland Revenue or of the Minister of Customs, as at this late hour particularly, to make the excuses they have made. They need not think for a moment that these excuses will be accepted by the people of Manitoba and the North-west. When this subject was under discussion before, I quoted the Act to show that it had been changed. These hon. gentlemen said that it had not been changed. But, if so, what is the explanation of the fact that the officers of the Customs Department did permit ten thousand barrels of bad oil to come into the country ? Was the oil inspected, or was it not ? It is evident, from the facts laid before the House by the Minister of Inland Revenue, that the department did not inspect it. After the oil was found to be bad, they recalled the oil. Seventy-five cases of that oil is found, and it is all right. I have just this to say, that it will take a great deal more than the statement that is read by the Minister pf Inland Revenue at this late moment of the session, to convince the people of Manitoba that the government has taken that care they should have taken hi regard to this matter.

So far as the Department of Customs is concerned, | Mr. BOYD.
the hon. gentleman should not say that the oil was not inspected. I informed the House that it was inspected. If it was not inspected, how does the hon. gentleman know that a personal test would not be effective? That shows the weakness of his objection. I say it was inspected.
I would ask the hon. gentleman, if it was inspected, of what good is his inspection ? The oil was no good, and if it was inspected he is in a worse position than when he started out.

If it is necessary, and that seems to be the idea of some hon. gentlemen here, that there should be new tests applied, that is a fair question for consideration. It is to be remembered, however, as the Minister of Inland Revenue tells us, I suppose from information in his possession, that if the test is [DOT]altered and a stronger test required, either in the gravity or tlie flash, the probability is that you will have to pay an increased price for oil. The question is whether, on account of one misshipment you would be willing that a test should be applied that will raise the price of oil used by the people of that country for all time to come. That is the question for these gentlemen to consider. Perhaps the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane), who seems to understand the question so thoroughly, would give us his advice on that point. *

I would be very happy to do so if I thought the minister would accept my advice. Iu our section of the country, I want to tell the hon. gentleinau that we have not been so long in the darkness as he thinks we have. It is evident enough to my mind that if the test is all right the hon. gentleman's officers are not all right. If the test is all right his inspectors do not know their business any more than the hon. gentleman knows his own business. We import oil in our section of the country, the officers of the Customs Department test the oil, and we never have any complaint. It occurs to me that the people might well pay a little more for their oil and have some more light than to pay what they do and sit in darkness. They are paying for oil that has no illuminating qualities at all. I think this is a serious matter, although we may treat it lightly, that the inhabitants of Manitoba should be paying for oil, when the officials of the department are not doing their duty. If they are doing their duty, the test they make is of no use.

This oil is American oil, brought in in tank vessels, and the Minister of Inland Revenue says that his officers simply have to test tile oil for gravity and flashing point. It comes in through the customs, and our officers have been furnished with the necessary instruments for determining the

gravity and the flash test according to the regulations laid down by the Inland Revenue Department. When the subject came up I made inquiry, and I was informed by the Commissioner that he had received from our officer a report, giving the actual test which he had taken. That convinced me that he had made the test. Now, this is what we have to consider. A mistake has occurred ; it may occur again. There must have been many shipments going on. You can conceive of nothing much more irritating and annoying for people living in the country and having to illuminate their dwellings, than that they should find the oil unsatisfactory. But the point I want to ascertain is whether hon. gentlemen wish the test altered and made stronger, as a result of which the price of oil would be increased.

Honourable Gentlemen of the Senate :
Gentlemen of the House of Commons:
In relieving you from further attendance in Parliament, I desire to thank you for the eare and attention given to your important duties.
The unusual number of Acts that have been passed incorporating industrial and railway companies may be taken as an evidence of the rapid progress that Canada is making in wealth and prosperity. Further proof of that satisfactory condition is afforded by the increase in the trade and revenue of the country.
It has been gratifying to note the unprecedented flow of immigrants from Europe and from the United States that are now seeking homes in Manitoba and in the North-west Territories. The rapidly increasing population in that fertile section of the Dominion must yearly add to the trade of the country.
The agreement entered into with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, when authorizing an increase of its capital, to expend over nine million dollars in providing additional rolling stock, will, it is hoped, materially diminish in the future the serious losses that have arisen from the insufficient supply of cars to carry the products of the west to eastern ports.	-
The amendments made to the Manitoba Grain Act authorizing the farmers in Manitoba and in the North-west Territories to erect flat warehouses for storing their grain at railway stations will, it is believed, be found to serve a useful purpose, and defeat any attempt to depress prices by combinations.
The growing population in the Yukon territory and the rapid development in the trade of that section of Canada amply justify the Act granting to its residents a representative in Parliament who will be authorized to speak for his constituency in all matters affecting the more important interests of that remote part of the Dominion.
Gentlemen of the. House of Commons :
I thank you in His Majesty's name for the liberal supplies you have granted for the public service.
Honourable Gentlemen of the Senate :
Gentlemen of the House of Commons:
In bidding you farewell, I desire to express the hope that when we meet next year we shall be able to again rejoice in the continued prosperity which now prevails over this wide Dominion.
